conversation_lines.text: Yeah, my legs kept getting bigger, and the redness on my left leg is worse now. It’s warm and painful too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We checked your labs and your white blood cell count is a bit high, which suggests some inflammation. Your BNP is also elevated, which points to fluid buildup from your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it my heart again? I thought I was doing okay on the water pill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like your body wasn’t getting rid of enough fluid at home. We’re going to restart IV furosemide to help reduce the swelling. We’ll also continue the IV vancomycin since your leg redness is worse—could still be infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on warfarin—did you check for a blood clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We did an ultrasound of your legs, and there’s no sign of a clot. Your PICC line was also checked with a chest X-ray—it’s in the right place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I didn’t want another clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine output was good overnight—you’ve already lost about 2 liters of fluid. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can breathe a little better, but my legs still hurt. Is the antibiotic helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s only been one day, so it may take a few more. We’re continuing vancomycin for a full 7-day course because of your history of tough infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My potassium was low last time—should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your potassium dropped to 3.4 this morning. We’re giving you supplements. It’s common with strong diuretics. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your swelling is improving. Edema is now 1+ instead of 2+. We’re switching from IV furosemide to your home medication, Bumetanide, but we’re reducing it to once daily to protect your potassium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll take less Bumex now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just 4 mg once a day instead of twice. We’ll monitor your weight daily. Call your doctor if you gain more than 3 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my seizure medicine? I’ve been feeling a bit wobbly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your phenytoin level yesterday. It’s higher than it should be—26.1, when the goal is around 15. That could be why you’re unsteady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so it’s not my legs? Should we lower the dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re reducing it from 900 mg to 700 mg daily. We’ll recheck the level in a week. A neurology consult said you’re safe to go home with this plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your leg redness and warmth are improving. No new wounds or weeping. We’re on day 5 of vancomycin—two more days and we’ll stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I won’t need more IV antibiotics at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we think the infection is cleared. We’re stopping vancomycin and adding a topical antifungal powder for any skin irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my warfarin? My INR was low last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We increased your warfarin to 8 mg daily. Your INR is now 2.0, which is in the target range. Keep taking it as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve lost over 6 kilograms since admission—great progress. Your breathing is better, and your legs are much less swollen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel lighter, for sure. But I still have some redness on my right leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s mild and not spreading. We think it’s from chronic skin changes, not infection. We’re adding loratadine for any itching or inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my eyes? They’ve been dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re prescribing artificial tears for that. It’s common and not serious. Use them as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today is day 7 of vancomycin. We’re stopping it now. Your labs show no signs of active infection, and your leg exam is much improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m done with IV meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll continue your regular pills. We’re also stopping Benadryl since it’s no longer needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was sleepy on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. Your weight is stable, breathing is good, and labs are improving. Your potassium is still a bit low at 3.4, so keep taking your supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What follow-up do I need?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need a chemistry panel and potassium check in a few days, and a phenytoin level in one week. Your PCP will coordinate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my PICC line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It stays in for now because you need frequent blood tests. Your home nurse will help, and it should be removed within a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re officially discharged. Your condition is stable, and you’re back to your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. What’s the main thing I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Weigh yourself every morning. If you gain more than 3 pounds in a day or two, call your doctor—it could mean fluid is building up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my phenytoin? I’ll take 700 mg now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 700 mg daily. Get the blood test in one week. If you feel more unsteady, let us know right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep taking your other meds as listed. Call if you have trouble breathing, leg swelling returns, or any new concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. A nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I restart CPAP? I know I don’t use it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It would help your breathing and heart long-term, but we know it’s hard with claustrophobia. Talk to your sleep doctor about alternatives if you’re open to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it. Maybe a different mask.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good idea. Small changes can make a big difference.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my leg skin—should I keep using the cream?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, use the triamcinolone cream as needed for rash. And now the miconazole powder for any redness or itching—apply it three times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll follow the list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’ve done really well. Just stay on top of the monitoring and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You came in today because of confusion and feeling off since your last discharge. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, since I got home, I’ve felt confused, like my thoughts are foggy. And my vision—sometimes the room feels like it’s spinning. I’ve had double vision too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any nausea or dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, some nausea, but no vomiting. And now I have this tremor in my left arm. It’s getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We checked your phenytoin level in the ER—it was 22.2, which is higher than the safe range. That could explain your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wait, I thought it was high when I left last time. They said it was 26.1 and 30.1. I didn’t feel right after that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It was already high, and even though they lowered your dose, the level stayed elevated. We think your body absorbed more of the medication because your swelling went down from the diuretics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I feel so strange? But I haven’t had a seizure, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we don’t think so. You’re still on topiramate, and now we’ve started Keppra, which also helps prevent seizures. Neurology agrees your symptoms are from phenytoin toxicity, not a seizure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. But why the tremor and nystagmus? I saw that word in the notes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nystagmus is the involuntary eye movement we saw. Both that and the tremor are classic signs of too much phenytoin. They should improve as the level drops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will that take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can take a few days to a week. We’ve stopped phenytoin completely and switched you to Keppra, which is safer and easier to manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my warfarin? I saw my INR was 1.9. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a bit low. Since you’re on warfarin for a past pulmonary embolism, we want your INR around 2 to 3. We’re increasing your dose from 5 mg to 8 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that be safe? I don’t want to bleed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor it closely. Actually, stopping phenytoin might increase your INR on its own, so we’ll check it again before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your phenytoin level dropped to 18.2 overnight. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! I do feel a little more clear-headed today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. We also did a chest X-ray to check the PICC line placed yesterday. It’s in the right spot—mid to lower SVC—no lung issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot about that. Was it needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just for easier access since you’re on multiple meds. It’ll be removed before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EEG showed a mildly slow brain pattern, but no seizure activity. It supports the idea of encephalopathy from the phenytoin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no seizure happened when my arms shook?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the EEG was clean. That shaking was likely a non-epileptic event or just part of the toxicity. Neurology thinks you’re doing well on Keppra.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. My tremor is still there, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should keep improving. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your phenytoin level is now 14.4. Still dropping. How’s your confusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I can think clearly now. The double vision is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent progress. The tremor might linger a bit longer, but it’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? I had some swelling in my arms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you an extra dose of IV furosemide. Your weight is stable now—145 kg. We’ll keep you on your usual Bumex and potassium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my pain? I’ve been holding off on the morphine because I was confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart your oxycodone for fibromyalgia. Since you’re more alert now, it’s safe to use as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your phenytoin level is now 10.3—back in the normal range. Great news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I feel so much better. Is it safe to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting close. Physical therapy saw you and says you’re steady on your feet. We just need your INR to settle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s it at now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: 2.1—perfect. We’ll keep you on 8 mg warfarin and you’ll need to check it again in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs look good. Your kidney function is stable, and potassium is a bit low at 3.2, so keep taking your supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. So I can go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll set up home services to help you adjust. You’ll follow up with neurology to monitor Keppra.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds? Everything else stays the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—same doses for thyroid, cholesterol, acid reflux, and your inhalers. Just no more phenytoin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m relieved. I didn’t like how it made me feel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your mental status is clear, you’re walking well, and all labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking Keppra and warfarin as prescribed. Weigh yourself daily—call if you gain more than 3 pounds. And follow up with neurology and your primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And if I feel confused again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back right away. But with Keppra, we don’t expect that. You’re on a safer med now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better already. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Clear-headed, no dizziness. My arm still trembles a little, but it’s much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. It may take a few more days. Keep up with your meds and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. The transport team will take you home shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and don’t hesitate to call if you have questions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Bye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. My legs have been swelling more and more over the past few weeks. I’ve gained about 18 pounds, and now my left leg is red and tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had swelling before due to lymphedema, correct? And you’ve been using compression stockings and diuretics at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. But this time, nothing’s helping. The swelling is up to my mid-shin, and the skin is weeping clear fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We also noticed redness on your left shin. Are you running a fever or feeling warm?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever, but the area is definitely warmer than the rest of my leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned about cellulitis, which is a skin infection. We’ll start you on IV antibiotics through your PICC line. We already confirmed it’s in the right place with an X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve had cellulitis before. But why is the swelling so bad this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into that. We stopped your oral diuretics for now and will try IV furosemide to help drain the fluid. But we have to be careful with your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had kidney issues before. My last creatinine was normal, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 1.0 when you came in, which is your baseline. We’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We gave you 160 mg of IV lasix yesterday. You’ve lost about 4 liters of fluid, and your swelling has improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. My legs feel a bit looser already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: However, your creatinine went up to 1.5. That means your kidneys are under stress. We’re holding off on more diuretics for now to protect them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t realize it could go up that fast. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a temporary issue, likely from the fluid shift. We’ll watch it and restart diuresis slowly if it improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine dropped to 1.3 today. That’s a good sign. We’re going to restart diuresis with a lasix drip and add boluses as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help with the swelling more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we aim to remove 1 to 2 liters per day. But we’ll stop if your creatinine rises again or if your potassium drops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on potassium supplements. Should I keep taking them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue the 20 mEq three times a day. We’ll check your levels regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your potassium is now 3.1 and bicarbonate is high at 33. This is called contraction alkalosis, which can happen with too much fluid loss.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can affect your heart rhythm, so we’ve stopped the lasix drip. We’ll go back to your home diuretics—bumetanide and spironolactone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I won’t lose more fluid in the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve done what we safely can. The swelling has improved, but we don’t want to risk your kidneys or electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your echocardiogram results. Your heart’s pumping function is normal, and there’s no major valve issue. So heart failure isn’t the main cause of your swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then what’s causing it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely your chronic lymphedema or venous stasis. The ultrasound didn’t show a blood clot, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had clots before. I’m glad it’s not that again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR has stayed in range at 2.4, so your warfarin is working well to prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count was high at 12.3 when you came in, but it’s now down to 10.1. The redness in your leg is also fading.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotic is working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, vancomycin is helping clear the infection. You’ll finish a full 7-day course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine peaked at 1.6 but is now back down to 1.4. That’s acceptable. We’ll discharge you on your home diuretics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to come back if the swelling gets worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, or if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day. Keep using ACE wraps and elevate your legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. Your infection is resolving, and your swelling is more manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You should see your primary care doctor in 3 days to check your electrolytes and kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the swelling clinic you mentioned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we recommend the lymphedema clinic at General Hospital. They can help with specialized compression and care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning show your WBC is now 9.9, and the redness is much fainter. You’re afebrile and doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. My legs aren’t as tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll finish your last dose of vancomycin today. Since you have a PICC, you could get IV antibiotics at home if needed, but it’s not necessary now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d rather not keep it if I don’t need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discuss with your PCP whether to keep it. For now, it stays in place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge is set for tomorrow. We’ll send instructions to your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on the same medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your usual meds are continued—levetiracetam, topiramate, warfarin, levothyroxine, and your pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the doxycycline I was taking for prevention?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We stopped it while you were on vancomycin. Your doctor will decide if you need to restart it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: your swelling has improved, infection is resolving, and labs are stable. You’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you develop fever, increased redness, shortness of breath, or rapid weight gain. Keep your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll weigh myself every morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Also, continue the ACE wraps and leg elevation during the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re finalizing your discharge. Your condition is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember to follow up in 3 days for labs and with your PCP about your swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your home health nurse will visit to help with your care. We’ve arranged that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I’ll be okay at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re doing well. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You're here because your legs have been swelling more than usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ve gotten so big and painful. I’ve gained over 20 pounds in a few weeks. My legs are tight, they blister, and when I lie down, the swelling goes into my belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve been taking your diuretics, the water pills, like usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, every day. I’m also on salt and fluid limits. Nothing’s helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. We’ll start IV diuretics to help pull off the extra fluid. We’ll monitor your labs closely. Your heart function will be checked with an echo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help me breathe better? I get short of breath just walking to the bathroom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, reducing the fluid should help. The chest X-ray shows no fluid in your lungs now, so that’s good. But your legs are holding a lot of fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also had chills the last couple days. Could I be fighting an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your urine and it’s clean. No fever now, and no signs of cellulitis. We’ll keep you on doxycycline as a preventive since you’ve had it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re going to place a PICC line so we can give your IV diuretics safely over the next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I had a blood clot in my arm before from a PICC.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand your concern. We’ll place it on the right side and confirm the position with an X-ray. We’ll also keep your warfarin going to prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC is in, but the tip was too high. We’ll reposition it later today under X-ray guidance to make sure it’s in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get some numbing medicine. It’s a quick procedure, and you’ll be awake. Most patients tolerate it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC is now correctly placed in the large vein near your heart. We’ve started the IV lasix.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I already feel a little less pressure in my legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your echo came back. Your heart is pumping well, so this swelling isn’t from heart failure. It’s likely lymphedema or venous stasis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why am I so swollen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your body isn’t draining fluid properly, and with your weight, the veins and lymph system are under strain. The IV diuretics will help reduce the load.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. My weight hasn’t gone down much though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. The scale might not reflect changes if fluid shifts. But your legs do look smaller. We’re tracking your intake and output too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your white count is still high, but no infection signs. We’ll keep the doxycycline as a preventive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from stress or inflammation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely. Your body is under strain from the fluid overload. It’s not an infection, so we won’t add antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was low yesterday. We’ve increased your warfarin dose to 8 mg daily to get it back in range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on warfarin for years. Why is it fluctuating now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Illness, diet changes, or other meds can affect it. We’ll monitor closely and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m told you had a seizure last night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t remember it. The nurse said I was twitching and frothing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looked like a generalized seizure. Your levetiracetam level was normal, but we think fluid overload may have triggered it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But my level was okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but sometimes even therapeutic levels aren’t enough during stress. We’re increasing your dose to 1500 mg twice daily to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine went up slightly, so we’re stopping the IV lasix. We don’t want to hurt your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the swelling might come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll switch to a higher dose of oral bumetanide—4 mg daily. You’ll also go to the diuretic clinic for occasional IV treatments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried about peeing all the time. Is 4 mg once a day okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with once daily to see how you tolerate it. We can adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your A1c came back at 6.4, which suggests prediabetes. We’ll monitor your sugars and encourage diet changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve always had borderline sugars. Should I see an endocrinologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Your PCP can follow this. Focus on low-sugar choices and monitoring weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your legs are still swollen, but less tender. The papules on your skin aren’t infected. We’ll keep the antifungal cream for itching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The canker sores on my tongue are bothering me. Any advice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re common with stress or vitamin changes. Rinse with warm salt water. They should heal in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning discharge in a couple days. Your INR is now 2.0, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I want to get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled follow-up with your PCP to check your levetiracetam level and INR. Call if your weight goes up more than 3 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the diuretic clinic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll contact you to reschedule. You may need IV diuretics every few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge weight is 156.1 kg. It hasn’t changed much, but your legs look better. The scale might not capture fluid shifts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I feel lighter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging tomorrow. You’ll go home with increased levetiracetam, warfarin, and bumetanide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep using oxycontin and morphine as needed. Also, we added stool softeners to prevent constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final labs look stable. Your potassium is good, and white count is still mildly high but not concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the swelling might come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might. That’s why we’re setting up the diuretic clinic and close follow-up. Watch your weight and symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home tomorrow. A nurse will call with instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’ll get you discharged by noon. Your final meds are ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Remember: weigh daily, take your meds, and follow up with your PCP and neurology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And the diuretic clinic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll call you. If swelling worsens before then, come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will take you to the lobby in 30 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m all packed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your warfarin is now 8 mg daily. Check your INR at the lab next week and fax it to your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep taking the levetiracetam twice a day. Neurology will see you in two months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I have the appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—I take the bumetanide once a day, not twice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We lowered it to once daily to reduce frequent urination. Call if swelling returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ride is here. Here’s your discharge summary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. My legs have been swelling up more and more over the last two and a half weeks. It’s gone all the way up to my belly now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had lymphedema before, right? Has it been worse than usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had it for years. But this time, even increasing my water pill didn’t help. I’ve gained about 10 pounds in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you’re on that 2-liter fluid limit and low-salt diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been sticking to it. My primary doctor and I tried bumping up my Bumex, but nothing changed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll start IV furosemide to help reduce the swelling. We’ll also check your heart and rule out a blood clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a PICC line placed last time. It’s still in my arm. Can we use that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll use it. We’ve already done a chest X-ray to confirm it’s in the right place—mid SVC, so it’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want it taken out. My veins are hard to access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’ll keep it for now, but we’ll talk later about long-term options like a port.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been wheezing a bit. Could that be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your lungs don’t show fluid on the X-ray, but we’ll monitor. You have a history of COPD, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and I know I should quit smoking. I’ve been trying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll give you support and resources. For now, we’ll start albuterol treatments as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night look stable. Your kidney function is okay, and no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My legs still hurt, though—especially the right shin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get an ultrasound today to check for a blood clot. But your exam doesn’t suggest cellulitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No redness or fever. Just a deep, throbbing pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely due to the swelling and stretch on the tissues. We can try gabapentin at night if you’re open to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d rather not. I’m already on a lot of meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fair enough. We’ll focus on reducing the swelling first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound came back. No DVT in your right leg. Limited views of the calf, but no clot seen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a blood clot. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We’ll keep you on IV lasix twice daily. Your weight’s down a little—good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can see my legs are a bit smaller. But I’m going to the bathroom a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. We’re removing extra fluid. We’ll put in a catheter so you don’t have to keep getting up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d prefer that. It’s hard to move with these swollen legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your INR was low yesterday—1.8. We’ve increased your warfarin from 7mg to 9mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on warfarin since my pulmonary embolism. I take it every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll check again in a couple days to make sure it’s in range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve noticed my mouth feels dry, and there’s white stuff on my tongue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be thrush, especially with the diuretics drying you out. We’ll start nystatin mouthwash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll use it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your Keppra level came back—19 mcg/mL. That’s in the therapeutic range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking 1000mg twice a day, but my neurologist prescribed 1500. Should I increase it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Since your level is good and you haven’t had a seizure, we’ll keep it as is for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had non-epileptic episodes too, so it’s hard to tell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue your current dose and follow up with neurology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine has gone up to 1.5. That means we need to slow down the IV diuretics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? My kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a sign we’re removing fluid too fast. We’ll stop IV lasix and restart your oral Bumex.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll go back to my regular pill?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 4mg daily. And we’ll keep you on fluid and salt restrictions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed your urine is cloudy. We sent a culture. Could be a UTI from the catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t felt any burning or urgency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes with a catheter, symptoms are masked. We’ll wait for results before starting antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture grew Citrobacter freundii. It’s sensitive to ciprofloxacin, so we’ll start that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a common bacteria in catheter infections. We’ll treat it for five days. We’ll also remove the catheter soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had it for a few days. I guess it makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.6—perfect. You’ll go home on 9mg warfarin daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ll keep my follow-up with my PCP for checks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, the rash under your left breast is looking better with the miconazole powder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, less red and itchy. I’ll keep using it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Swelling’s improved, no more wheezing, and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if all goes well. We’ll discharge you with ciprofloxacin for five days and your regular meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the PICC line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can keep it, but we strongly recommend discussing a port or removal with your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. We’ll review your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue Bumex, warfarin, and ciprofloxacin. Follow low salt and fluids—1500cc daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And see my primary doctor for follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we strongly recommend you see a lymphedema clinic for long-term management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll look into that. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if swelling worsens or you have fever, pain, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll try to quit smoking for good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great goal. We’re here to support you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your prescriptions and discharge papers shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have your ride called. Take it easy, and follow up as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest and keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Ms. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will assist you with discharge prep now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll wait for her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ll make the appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I fell at home while cleaning the floor. Landed on my right leg. Since then, it’s gotten really red, warm, and swollen—more than usual. I’ve had this before, like cellulitis flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, chills, or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever. Just the leg pain and my back acting up again. And I’ve gained weight—up to 352 pounds. I can barely walk now, feels like I’m carrying fluid on my legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll check your vitals and get some labs. Your breathing has a bit of wheeze, but you’re not short of breath. We’ll also do a chest X-ray to make sure the fluid isn’t in your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’ve been using my walker more because of the swelling. Normally I just use a cane.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray is back. No signs of fluid in the lungs, which is good. But your white blood cell count is high—15.2—suggesting infection in your leg. We’ll start IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on doxycycline for years to prevent these flares. Why isn’t it working now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes bacteria become resistant, or the infection is more severe. We’re starting vancomycin because it covers more types of bacteria, especially since you’re on long-term doxycycline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about the swelling? I feel so heavy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve gained nearly 20 pounds since your last dry weight. We think it’s due to your heart not relaxing properly—diastolic dysfunction. We’ll start IV furosemide twice a day to help you pass the extra fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s heart-related? But I’m not short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Some people feel it mostly in their legs. The heart isn’t filling well, so fluid backs up. Your proBNP is only 110, which is mild, but your exam and weight gain support this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve started to urinate more—great sign. We’re seeing good diuresis. Your creatinine was 1.4 yesterday, so we’re watching your kidneys closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? My kidneys were an issue last time I was here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s slightly elevated, but stable. We’ll keep the IV lasix but monitor your labs daily. We don’t want to push too hard and hurt your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I’ve got these sores in my mouth and a rash where the IV is. Could it be from the vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Vancomycin can cause skin reactions and mouth ulcers in some people. We’ll stop it and switch to clindamycin, which also treats your cellulitis but is gentler on your skin and mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. The mouth sores are really painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you nystatin mouthwash to soothe the ulcers. Swish and spit four times a day as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is coming down—13.2 today. That means the antibiotics are working. You’ve also lost about 5 pounds—great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel a bit lighter. Can I walk more now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can try with assistance. Keep using the walker. The redness in your leg is improving, but it’s still tender. No pus or spreading, so that’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about going home. I live alone, and my aide was gone for a week. She said I looked really swollen when she came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re arranging home health services. A nurse will check your leg, help with meds, and monitor your weight daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps. And my warfarin? I’m on 6 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing warfarin. No issues with your INR so far. You have a history of DVT and PE, so staying on it is crucial.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re down to 348 pounds—close to your target. Creatinine improved to 1.2. We’ll switch you to oral bumetanide at 3 mg twice a day when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was only taking 2 mg a few times a week before. Is 3 mg twice a day safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ll monitor your potassium. You’re on spironolactone and potassium supplements, so we’ll check levels with your outpatient labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My mouth feels better with the nystatin. Should I keep using it after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use it as needed for pain. It’s not an antibiotic, just helps soothe the sores. Stop when you’re comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your leg is less red and warm. WBC is stable. You’re making great progress. We’ll keep clindamycin IV for a few more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need IV antibiotics at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for about a week. Home health will bring the IV meds and teach you or your aide how to give them safely through your PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still using my albuterol inhaler sometimes. Is my lung issue related to all this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have chronic airway obstruction, likely from obesity and possibly asthma. The wheezing isn’t worse, so we’ll keep your inhalers as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning discharge in a couple of days. You’re close to your weight goal, infection is improving, and you’re moving better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Weigh yourself every morning. If you gain 3 pounds in a day or 5 in a week, call your doctor. Watch for increased leg redness, fever, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on topiramate and levetiracetam for years. Any changes there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No changes. You have seizure disorder and non-epileptic events. Keep taking both meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning are good. Creatinine 1.2, potassium 3.6. We’ll keep your diuretics and continue clindamycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my thyroid? I take levothyroxine daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue 50 mcg daily. No signs of under- or overactive thyroid. We’ll check TSH at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using morphine and oxycontin for pain. Is that okay long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have chronic back and leg pain. These are appropriate for now. Just take them as prescribed and avoid alcohol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night’s weight was 348 pounds—perfect. We’ll discharge you tomorrow morning if all stays on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What meds will I go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue warfarin, spironolactone, bumetanide 3 mg twice a day, and your seizure meds. Clindamycin IV for a week, plus nystatin for mouth sores as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another PICC line flush?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re sending you home with saline and heparin flushes. Home health will help with that to keep the line working and prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I should lose weight. Any advice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Focus on small steps. Low-sodium diet, daily weights, and staying active as you can. Your PCP can refer you to nutrition and lymphedema clinics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today. Your infection and fluid overload are much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What’s the plan for follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your primary doctor in a week. They’ll check your INR and chemistry panel. Home health will visit three times this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my leg? Should I keep it elevated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, elevate when sitting. Wear compression if you can tolerate it. Watch for redness or warmth returning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if anything changes. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. The discharge team will bring your instructions and prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep using your EpiPen if you have a severe allergic reaction. And avoid NSAIDs and aspirin—they’re on your allergy list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I know. I use acetaminophen instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. That’s much safer with your warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my CPAP? I don’t use it much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Try to use it nightly. Sleep apnea makes heart strain worse. Your PCP can help troubleshoot comfort issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll give it another try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all for now. Rest up, and we’ll get you home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The nurse will be in shortly to assist with discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll wait.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your esomeprazole for GERD. Keep taking it daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I haven’t missed a dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That helps protect your stomach, especially with the pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll let the team know you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You came in because your legs have been swelling more than usual. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, over the past week, my legs have gotten much heavier and swollen, up to my thighs. I’ve been using wraps and elevation, but it’s not helping like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned some shortness of breath too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, when I walk, I get winded faster than normal. But no chest pain or palpitations.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your labs show your white blood cell count is a bit high, but you’re not running a fever. Your BNP, which checks for heart strain, is normal, and your chest X-ray shows no fluid in the lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely congestive heart failure. Given your history of lymphedema and obesity, this is probably a flare-up of that. But you are responding to diuretics, so there may be a small heart component.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking my Bumex every day. Why isn’t it working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes with severe lymphedema, oral diuretics aren’t enough. We’re starting IV furosemide to help pull off more fluid, but we’ll watch your kidney function closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We reviewed your foot X-ray—no fracture. The swelling is consistent with lymphedema. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My right foot is a bit red between the toes. Could that be infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a concern. Given your history of frequent cellulitis, we’ll start IV clindamycin just in case, even though it may just be a lymphedema flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on doxycycline for prevention. Should I keep that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. We’ll continue your home doxycycline. The IV antibiotic is extra protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine went up a little yesterday, so we’re adjusting your furosemide dose. We don’t want to hurt your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s mild and expected with aggressive diuresis. We’re just being cautious. Your swelling is improving, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt a little confused last night. I couldn’t speak clearly for a few minutes. My arm twitched.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I heard about that. We consulted neurology. They don’t think it was a seizure. You’ve had similar episodes in the past during fluid overload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m on my seizure meds. Levetiracetam and topiramate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’re keeping them the same. Sometimes volume changes affect medication levels. We sent a Keppra level, but it’s still pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could the new gabapentin cause confusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. It can cause drowsiness, especially when started. We’ll watch that. But it’s helping your nerve pain, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the shooting pain in my leg is better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count has come down a bit—from 14.4 to 12.5. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. You’ve been afebrile, and the chest X-ray is clear. Smoking can raise white counts, and you’re a smoker, so that may be contributing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using the nicotine patch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We started the 21 mg patch. Given your seizure history, we can’t use certain other smoking cessation drugs, but the patch is safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping the IV clindamycin. After six days, there’s no clear sign of cellulitis, and no improvement suggests it wasn’t needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it was just lymphedema?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mostly. The redness and warmth were subtle, and no fever or spreading infection. We’ll keep you on doxycycline for prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve noticed my mouth feels sore. I think I have thrush.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see white patches on your tongue. That’s thrush. We’ll start nystatin mouthwash three times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Antibiotics can disrupt normal mouth flora. Also, chronic conditions and medications increase risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your weight is fluctuating—158.3, then 157.2—but overall, your swelling is less. You’re close to your dry weight of 153.3 kg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel puffy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Lymphedema fluid is stubborn. Wrapping and elevation help. We’ll keep you on spironolactone and bumetanide at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your Keppra level came back normal. That supports the neurology team’s view—your episode wasn’t a seizure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what was it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely a mix of fluid overload, sedating meds like gabapentin, and your history of non-epileptic events. Still, we recommend a neurology follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make the appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in a few days. You’re stable, and your labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need home care?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, home health will help with wound care, medication checks, and monitoring your weight and legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still tired in the mornings. Is my sleep apnea worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. You’re not on CPAP at home, and with obesity, OSA can contribute to fatigue. We didn’t start CPAP here, but it’s something to discuss with your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is stable at 1.4. We’ll keep your diuretics as prescribed and monitor at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I weigh myself daily?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Call your doctor if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day or notice increased swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Discharge is tomorrow. We’re sending you home on gabapentin for nerve pain, nystatin for thrush, and all your usual meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the gabapentin make me too sleepy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might at first. We started low. If it’s too sedating, talk to your doctor about adjusting it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And I’ll keep the nicotine patch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It’s a good step. Avoid smoking—it worsens swelling and lung function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your swelling has improved, no signs of infection, and you’re neurologically stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up with neurology and my primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Keep wrapping your legs, take your diuretics, and call if anything changes. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in tonight for worsening leg swelling and redness. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my legs have been swelling more over the past week. They’re red and warm, especially on the lower parts. My primary doctor saw me yesterday and said it might be cellulitis, so he started me on IV antibiotics through my PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And how’s the redness been since starting the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s a little better, but now two of my toes are getting redder. I’m also feeling short of breath when I walk, and I’ve had some wheezing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. We’ll monitor that. Your vitals are stable, and your chest X-ray came back clear, so it doesn’t look like heart failure is the main issue. We’ll continue the IV clindamycin for the infection and start IV furosemide to help with the swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on bumetanide at home—4 mg daily. I was on every other day for a bit, but when the swelling came back, I went back to daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll use stronger IV diuretics here to help get the fluid off faster. We also noticed your INR was high when we checked—likely because of the antibiotics affecting your warfarin. We’ll hold the warfarin for now and start a heparin drip to keep your blood thinning safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I didn’t know antibiotics could do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, some can. We’ll watch it closely and restart your warfarin when it’s safe. For now, focus on resting and letting the treatment work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. The swelling hasn’t gone down much, but my breathing feels a bit easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your white blood cell count is elevated, which supports the infection. But your kidney function is a little worse—creatinine went up from 1.2 to 1.4. So we’re adjusting your diuretic to avoid stressing your kidneys too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s mild and expected with aggressive diuresis. We’re monitoring it closely. We’ve switched from IV furosemide twice daily to a continuous drip to be gentler on your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your redness is improving, which is a good sign the antibiotics are working. You’re on day two of IV clindamycin, and we’ll continue for a full 10-day course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about my weight? I think I gained about 9 pounds before coming in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You weighed 352.7 pounds on admission. We’re tracking daily weights. So far, you’ve lost about 2 pounds, which is slow but expected given how hard it is to remove fluid in lymphedema.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s frustrating. I eat low salt and take my meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Lymphedema makes fluid control very tough. We’ll keep working on it. Also, we noticed you have oral thrush—white patches in your mouth. Were you on nystatin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to fluconazole, an oral antifungal. It works better for thrush and should clear it up in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is coming down. It was 4.2 on admission, now it’s 2.8. We’re restarting your warfarin at 7 mg daily and will keep checking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With your history of DVT and PE, we have to be careful. The ultrasound showed no new clots, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is stable, and you’re using your inhalers as needed. The wheezing is mild. We’ll keep monitoring your COPD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t needed them much today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Also, we’re continuing your high-dose pain meds for fibromyalgia, but the team noted you’ve been very sleepy. We’ll discuss this with your PCP after discharge to see if adjustments are needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I’m on a lot, but the pain is real.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe you. It’s just about balancing pain control with safety. We’ll make sure your PCP has all the details.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your redness is much better, and the new redness in your toes hasn’t spread. That’s a good sign the infection is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. My legs still hurt, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain is likely from the swelling and skin changes. We’ll keep managing it with your current meds and compression as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your weight is now 160.4 kg—down about 1 kg from admission. It’s slow, but we’re making progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Only a kilo? I feel like I should be losing more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With severe lymphedema and obesity, fluid is very hard to remove. We’ve had to slow down the diuretics to protect your kidneys. It’s a balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess I’ll have to be patient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your thrush is improving. You’re on day four of fluconazole—just a few more doses to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My mouth feels better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re also keeping you on the nicotine patch since you’re not smoking in the hospital. Your PCP can help with long-term cessation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like to quit, honestly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great goal. We’ll make a note to discuss support options at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
